patient_information: A 38-year-old European expatriate male with an unremarkable previous medical history. He reports having sexual contact only with his wife.
chief_complaint: Progressive constipation and difficulty passing urine for the past 3 weeks.
history_of_present_illness: For three weeks, the patient experienced progressive difficulty passing urine, requiring increasing abdominal pressure to pass small amounts, associated with lower abdominal discomfort, abnormal sensations in the groins and genitals, and erectile dysfunction. He denied weakness, dysaesthesia, or loss of sensation in his legs, but felt that his walking was abnormal in an unspecified way. He had no backache. Over the past two months, he had unintentional weight loss of 8kg and fatigue, without fever or night sweats. One week prior to presentation, he noticed reddish discoloration of his urine without painful micturition or fever, for which he received four types of medication from a local clinic.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The patient is a European expatriate living in Malawi. He had a history of swimming regularly in Lake Malawi.
physical_exam: The patient appeared healthy. General examination was normal except for a palpable bladder. A rectal examination revealed a low anal sphincter tone, and the genital examination was normal. Neurological examination showed lively, symmetrical tendon reflexes in the legs without clonus or pathological plantar reflexes, with no other abnormalities.
labs_and_diagnostics: Urine microscopy from a local clinic one week prior had identified Schistosoma haematobium eggs. A full blood count showed a normal absolute WBC of 9 x 10^9/L but with a relative eosinophilia of 21.8% and an absolute eosinophil count of 1.15 x 10^9/L. ALT was slightly elevated, while creatinine and CRP were normal. HIV and VDRL tests were negative. Repeat stool and urine microscopy were normal. An abdominal ultrasound showed a large bladder residue. An MRI scan of the spinal cord revealed an enhancing 1cm lesion at the anterior aspect of the conus medullaris with associated oedema extending to the T9 level, as well as nodular thickening of the bladder wall.
differential_diagnosis: The patient's presentation was compatible with a conus syndrome. The most important differential diagnosis considered was spinal cord schistosomiasis. Other infections considered were spinal tuberculosis, a spinal abscess, and neurosyphilis. A tumour or metastases impinging on the conus medullaris was also a possibility to be ruled out.
management_and_clinical_course: The patient had previously been treated at a local clinic with praziquantel, ciprofloxacin, buscopan, and bisacodyl. After diagnosis, he required urinary catheterization for 2 weeks. He was treated with a second course of praziquantel and a course of high-dose prednisolone which was tapered off over 2 months. He made a full recovery and remained well at over 2 years of follow-up.
final_diagnosis: The patient was diagnosed with spinal cord schistosomiasis due to Schistosoma haematobium, presenting as a conus syndrome. The diagnosis was based on the prior identification of S. haematobium eggs in his urine, supported by significant peripheral eosinophilia, a history of fresh water exposure in Lake Malawi, and characteristic MRI findings of an enhancing lesion in the conus medullaris and bladder wall thickening.
